record.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation
record.issuing_body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) and Office for Artificial Intelligence
record.summary: White paper setting out the UK's context-based approach to AI regulation. Existing regulators are to apply five cross-sectoral principles (safety, security and robustness; appropriate transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress), issued at first on a non-statutory basis, with a statutory duty on regulators to have due regard to them anticipated later if needed. New central functions, including risk monitoring and horizon scanning, support regulators, and the paper considers how foundation models fit the framework.
record.notes: Presented to Parliament as Command Paper CP 815 and published with an impact assessment and a consultation, which closed on 21 June 2023. A correction slip of 4 July 2023 corrected minor errors in Annex C, and the GOV.UK page was last updated on 3 August 2023. GOV.UK shows it as published under the 2022 to 2024 Sunak Conservative government.

verification.note: Stored and read in this run: the GOV.UK publication page (last checked 17 Oct 2026, unchanged since 11 Oct) and the web-ready and print-ready PDFs of the white paper. They confirm the title, CP 815, publication on 29 March 2023, the last update of 3 August 2023 (Annex C correction), the issuers and the content in the summary; the page carries no withdrawal notice. Version 1's statement that the approach remains the basis of UK policy and that no comprehensive UK AI bill had been introduced by October 2026 is not in these sources and was removed from the notes; the government's 2024 response is the related record GB-04.

summary.quote: Our framework is underpinned by five principles to guide and inform the responsible development and use of AI in all sectors of the economy:
Safety, security and robustness o Appropriate transparency and explainability o Fairness o Accountability and governance o Contestability and redress
we anticipate introducing a statutory duty on regulators requiring them to have due regard to the principles.
we will not move to introduce such a statutory duty if our monitoring of the framework shows that implementation is effective without the need to legislate.
we will deliver a range of central functions, including horizon scanning and risk monitoring
